A 46-yr-old female (165 cm, 70 kg) with SPS
was scheduled for a lumpectomy and sentinel lymph node
biopsy following diagnosis of breast (left) cancer. Six years

prior to surgery she was diagnosed with SPS that
manifested as muscle spasms and episodes of rigidity
provoked by anxiety or by certain activities such as
stretching. Investigation for SPS conﬁrmed elevated GAD
antibodies in her cerebrospinal ﬂuid (anti-GAD antibodies
[ 100), and at the time of surgery her medical treatment
included oral diazepam 5 mg and azathioprine 50 mg twice
daily. Baclofen was discontinued by her neurologist two
years prior to surgery, and she had received monthly iv
immunoglobulin therapy for 1.5 years (last treatment ﬁve
years prior to surgery). Her last SPS exacerbation, one year
prior to surgery, was thought to be triggered by work-
related anxiety. Concomitant medical conditions included
type I diabetes (blood glucose well-controlled; no
symptoms of peripheral neuropathy in upper or lower
extremities), generalized anxiety disorder and
gastroesophageal reﬂux. Non SPS-related medications
included insulin and pantoprazole. She was a non-smoker
and had no cardiovascular or respiratory comorbidities. She
had no prior surgical history. One month prior to surgery, a
neurologic exam (requested by the surgeon for baseline
functional assessment) identiﬁed only mild limitations of
neck movement and shoulder abduction.
The patient was interviewed in the preoperative clinic
three days before surgery (S. B. B). On physical exam, the
airway was reassuring (normal range of motion of head,
neck, and jaw; normal thyromental distance; full set of
teeth; Mallampati 2) and laboratory ﬁndings (complete
blood count, blood chemistry, coagulation proﬁle) as well
as an electrocardiogram (EKG) were within normal
parameters. The patient was well informed about
anesthesia-related SPS concerns including the risk of
postoperative hypotonia following general anesthesia.

The option of a strictly regional/local anesthesia technique
was not discussed as experience with this approach (for
combined breast surgery and axillary lymph node
dissection) is lacking at our hospital.
Following insertion of an 18G catheter into a right
upper-extremity vein (left arm draped for surgery),
standard monitors were applied (3-lead EKG, noninvasive
blood pressure cuff [lower limb so as to not interfere with
intravenous infusions], pulse oximeter, Bispectral Index
TM
(BISTM; Covidien/Medtronic, Minneapolis, MN, USA)
monitor electrodes, and train-of-four (TOF) monitor
(Philips [Amsterdam, the Netherlands] 865383 IntelliVue
Neuromuscular Transmission module accelerometer
afﬁxed to thumb; ulnar nerve stimulation, no thumb pre-
load). Premedication consisted of midazolam 2.0 mg
(anxiolytic) and glycopyrrolate 0.3 mg (antisialagogue)
while the patient was preoxygenated with 100% oxygen via
a snug-ﬁtting face mask. Loss of consciousness was
achieved with propofol 200 mg, lidocaine 80 mg,
sufentanil 15 lg, and remifentanil 100 lg; this was
followed by dexamethasone 8 mg for postoperative
nausea and vomiting (PONV) prophylaxis and
clindamycin 600 mg. Although bag-and-mask ventilation
was performed without difﬁculty, insertion of the
laryngoscope blade into the oropharynx required
facilitation with 20 mg rocuronium; TOF calibration was
done just prior to rocuronium administration.
Subsequently, oral intubation was easily achieved (grade
2 Cormack–Lehane view, #7.0 endotracheal tube). General
anesthesia was maintained by continuous infusion of
propofol (100–200 lg/C1kg
-1/C1min-1, titrated to BIS values
between 40 and 60) and remifentanil infusion

(0.1 lg/C1kg-1/C1min-1, titrated to maintain systemic arterial
pressure within 20% of baseline. No additional muscle
relaxant was administered to help ensure that nerves could
be identiﬁed during axillary lymph node dissection by
electrocautery-elicited muscle contraction. Normothermia
was maintained with a lower-body forced-air warming
blanket.
Maintenance of an appropriate depth of anesthesia and
stability of cardiovascular parameters during surgery were
achieved without incident. Train-of-four returned to 4/4
(100%) within 30 min of rocuronium administration. The
surgery was uneventful and lasted one hour and 45 min, at
which time the infusions were discontinued. Ondansetron
4 mg was administered for further PONV prophylaxis.
Upon emergence, the patient followed commands but had a
weak hand grip, was unable to lift her head or extremities,
and spontaneous ventilation consisted of shallow tidal
volumes (50–150 ml). Sugammadex 250 mg was then
administered and reversal of muscle weakness was
observed within about two minutes. The patient was
subsequently extubated in the operating room and
transferred to the postanesthesia care unit without
incident. The patient was discharged home a few hours
afterwards. Follow-up four days later revealed a smooth
postoperative course at home without exacerbation of SPS
symptoms or any sign of muscle weakness.
